draft.title: Herd immunity
card: A pathogen spreads when an infected person passes it to someone who is susceptible, meaning not immune. Each immune person in a community is a dead end for the pathogen.
Herd immunity happens when enough of a population is immune that each case infects, on average, fewer than one other person. The outbreak then dies out or stays small.
This protects people who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies or people with weakened immune systems. They are shielded because the pathogen rarely reaches them.

How many people must be immune depends on how easily the pathogen spreads. A very contagious disease such as measles needs a higher share immune than a less contagious one. If vaccination rates fall below that level, outbreaks become more likely.
draft.remember: Herd immunity works because immune people block the spread, so the unprotected are exposed less often.

a.q: How does herd immunity protect a baby who is too young to be vaccinated?
opts: Immune people around the baby rarely pass the pathogen on
The baby's body copies the immunity of nearby people
The pathogen is destroyed in every person in the community
Vaccinated people pass memory cells to the baby by contact
a.why: When most people nearby are immune, the pathogen has few chances to reach the baby. The baby is not made immune, so the protection depends on others staying immune. Immunity cannot be passed on by contact.
a.clue: Think about who the pathogen can reach, not about the baby's own body.

b.q: In a town, the share of children vaccinated against measles falls well below the level needed for herd immunity. What is the most likely result?
opts: Measles can spread more easily, even to unvaccinated people
Measles can no longer spread to vaccinated children
Measles becomes less contagious in the town
Unvaccinated people become immune by being nearby
b.why: With fewer immune people, each case has more susceptible people to infect, so outbreaks become more likely. Unvaccinated people lose the shield and are exposed more often. Being near immune people no longer helps once there are too few of them, and it never makes someone immune.
b.clue: What happens to the dead ends when fewer people are immune?

a.best: Immune people around the baby rarely pass the pathogen on

b.best: Measles can spread more easily, even to unvaccinated people

problems.detail: The correct option says measles spreads 'even to unvaccinated people'. 'Even' wrongly suggests unvaccinated people are an unlikely target, when they are the people most at risk. Reword to 'especially to unvaccinated people' or 'mainly to unvaccinated people'.

problems.detail: The why says 'Immunity cannot be passed on by contact.' This is overstated. Year 12 students learn natural passive immunity, where a mother's antibodies reach the baby through the placenta or breast milk. The point to make is that memory cells are not passed on, and that herd immunity does not work by giving the baby immunity.
